citations.quote: Recently there has been an increasing demand for a rapid mission concept generation capability for CubeSats, NanoSats, and SmallSats at JPL and in the broader community in the Concept Maturity Level (CML) 2-5 range.

This concurrent team-based approach provides rapid turnaround for small spacecraft mission and system early concept studies. The process is adaptable to a wide variety of CubeSat, NanoSat, and SmallSat customers and mission applications.

The Team Xc capability has been applied to several studies and extended to cover a large breadth of missions spanning applications including Earth science, planetary science, astrophysics, and technology demonstration.

The 'c' in Team Xc originally stood for CubeSat. However, during the development phase the core team realized the need for flexibility in form factor and therefore expanded the team's capability to accommodate the technical design of non-standard NanoSats and SmallSats (defined here to be less than or equal to 50 kg).

The teams processes build off the experiences of Team X [4][5], JPL's concurrent engineering team for rapid design and analysis of space mission concepts, with the processes tailored and design tools created to embrace the high-risk low-cost paradigm spearheaded by the CubeSat community.

Unlike the typical Earth-orbiting CubeSat mission concepts seen in the industry, Team Xc is not limited by a particular platform or mission destination. Space mission concepts utilizing various platforms, standards and form factors to numerous destinations in the Solar System are designed and evaluated by the team.
An average Team Xc study takes two weeks with two study sessions and costs the equivalent of one work-month of a full-time employee.

The team would then assess the feasibility of the mission concept within the known constraints such as mass, power, volume, CubeSat design requirements, etc., as well as known capabilities such as propulsion, attitude control, etc.
During CML 2 studies, subsystem experts use low-fidelity, rapid design tools and first-order sizing calculations to determine whether or not the concept is feasible.

During the course of the study, Team Xc develops a preliminary concept of operations for the mission, and provides the customer team with the following set (or subset) of products: Master Equipment List (MEL), Power Equipment List (PEL), power modes, orbit/trajectory design, high-level mission cost range, science/mission requirements and traceability, schedule or project timeline, link budget, End-to-End Information System (EEIS) design, identification of ground stations, assessment of level of complexity of software, risk analysis, identification of heritage missions and/or components, and structural design.
The Team Xc study process consists of planning meetings, study concurrent design sessions, and product generation. Each study process is tailored to the customer's desired results.

Before each study, the Team Xc facilitator and systems engineer conduct a planning meeting with the customer team to understand the goals of the study sessions. This allows the Team Xc staff to determine which subsystem experts will be needed in each session, how many sessions will be required to converge on a solution, and if any preliminary work needs to occur before the study session.

The collaborative, concurrent design sessions are typically constrained to three hours each. This limitation helps establish a pace for the study; since the studies are focused on Pre-Phase A designs for small satellite systems, the fast pace of the study sessions encourages and supports the subsystem experts to converge on a design with rapid design methods and tools.

Design sessions usually consist of 2-3 sessions within 1 week, with 7 to 10 subsystem/discipline experts depending on the complexity of the concept. Each expert operates their own specific design models.

The systems engineers are tasked with identifying the design trade loops going on between subsystems and coordinate the cross-cutting problem solving. The lead systems engineer also tracks the instantaneous mass, volume, and power best estimates from the subsystem chairs and verifies that they are consistent with the customer's requirements (see Figure 3).

During the session, the lead systems engineer will pause the study session and go around the room to allow each subsystem chair to report on the status of their work (see Figure 2). This break also allows the team to view the current roll-ups of the combined mass and power budgets and adjust the direction of the study, if required.

Studies are considered to be converged at the end of the final session, assuming no critical trade or design remains unfinished. Depending on the customer's needs, Team Xc can provide in-session comments or a refined post-session final report. In-session comments are generated as the final session wraps up and can provide a general "go" or "no-go" feasibility analysis of the study. The preliminary results are typically delivered to the customer within 24 hours after the conclusion of the sessions.

Each subsystem expert has templates to generate slides or text reports that focus on assumptions and decisions that were made during the study, how each subsystem meets the customer's requirements, lists generated technical information and component selection, and spells out major concerns and future work. These reports are compiled by the systems engineers and proofread for consistency and missing pieces across all subsystems. This iterative report generation process allows for subsystem chairs to revisit their designs and fix minor issues with the systems engineering team in the loop. Within one week after the conclusion of the study, the customer is presented with a draft report from the study for review, and one week later the final report is sent out.

Team Xc is staying upto-date with CubeSats, NanoSat and SmallSat experiences and developments within JPL and the community at large in order to continuously reflect the knowledge gained from flight projects in the improvement of its design models.

Many of the discipline experts, subsets of the tools, facilities, and many of the concurrent engineering techniques and best practices are shared by Team Xc. However, there are some key differences between the study approaches and tools used by each of the teams, as well.

Similar to Team X, Team Xc's models use Microsoft Excel workbooks as the front-end tool for communicating through a server to exchange parameters with options for running integrated MATLAB and Python scripts.

For example, the power design workbook has formulas and tools that govern power generation, solar array sizing, battery sizing, power modes, bus current utilization, depth of discharge analysis, and end-of-life deterioration effects.

Not all Team Xc design tools are self-contained; design tools such as the telecom model, require the discipline expert to run simulations in MATLAB and STK to generate design data, which must then be manually copied over into the Excel workbook. JPL's Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) team within the JPL Innovation Foundry is working with Team Xc to evolve JPL's concurrent engineering capabilities and solve these model integration challenges.

While the verification and validation of the domain (technical and cost) models is the responsibility of each subsystem subject matter expert, the MBSE effort is less concerned with the content of the domain models and is instead focused on improving the user's experience when running the models together. Rather than a monolithic workbook with many different formula-based tools, MBSE wrappers can interface with Excel, STK, MATLAB, CAD tools, scripting languages, and many other platforms using a common input and output scheme for attributes. These attributes can be shared between tools automatically.

In the current power design workbook, the discipline expert must step through the design serially to manually converge on the design. With the wrapper-based MBSE approach, the interconnected models can be run quickly through a wide range of potential values within the trade space. The results can be rapidly interpreted through plots, formulas, or comparisons that allow converged design points to be quickly iterated in order to identify the sensitivities in the design. While Team Xc maintains a working "operational" version of the models at all time, the team is continuously working in parallel with the MBSE effort to improve the efficiency and the way the models interoperate during design sessions and converge on solutions.
